summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: John Beverley
  • Channel: John Beverley
  • Main topic: How philosophical training in ontology engineering and formal ontologies provides unique value in solving big data interoperability challenges.
  • Purpose: To explain the value philosophers bring to ontology engineering, how ontologies solve big data interoperability challenges, and why demand for ontologists is growing. John Beverley, Assistant Professor at the University of Buffalo and VP of the National Center for Ontological Research (NCOR), presents on 'How to Do Things with Ontologies.' He discusses big data problems such as volume, velocity, variety, and veracity, focusing on information silos caused by incompatible storage systems and lack of standardized semantics. He introduces ontologies as formally well-defined, machine-interpretable controlled vocabularies and explains the role of Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) as a top-level architecture rooted in philosophical realism. Throughout the talk and subsequent Q&A, Beverley emphasizes why philosophers are uniquely suited for ontology engineering due to their training in conceptual analysis, formal logic, and handling disparate usage across scientific and industrial domains.

Topic Map

Big Data Problems and Information Silos

  • Explanation: Examining the challenges of big data, including huge volume (over 147 zettabytes stored by 2022), high velocity, variety of formats (JSON-LD, XML), and veracity issues leading to conflicting data and information silos that cannot be easily integrated.
  • Key claims:
    • Data is growing exponentially, making manual integration and human creativity insufficient.
    • Information silos cause data fragmentation, redundancy, bottlenecks, and incompatibility across repositories.
    • Lack of interoperability costs industrial datasets between $21-43 billion, with mid-size companies spending $20-50 million annually.
  • Examples:
    • Data stored in docx files or text files in one database versus another incompatible system.
    • Disagreements between trusted academic journal articles or philosophical debates creating conflicting data.
  • Terminology:
    • information silos
    • interoperability
    • zettabytes
    • data fragmentation
    • veracity
  • Why it matters: Information silos prevent organizations from extracting true value from data, leading to massive financial waste and operational bottlenecks.

Ontology Solutions and the Promise of Ontology Engineering

  • Explanation: Ontologies serve as known solutions to information silo challenges by acting as formally well-defined, machine-interpretable controlled vocabularies that make implicit meanings explicit and provide a semantic layer.
  • Key claims:
    • Ontologies provide a lingua franca across silos, reducing fragmentation and redundancy.
    • They promote automated data integration, standardizing querying and mapping.
    • Ontologies hit all five 'V's of big data: volume, velocity, variety, veracity, and value.
  • Examples:
    • The Gene Ontology (GO) consortium, started in 1998 alongside the human genome project to coordinate biological terminology.
    • Government and industry adoption of ontologies in AI roadmaps (DARPA, DHS, NIST, Gardner).
  • Terminology:
    • ontology
    • semantic layer
    • lingua franca
    • Gene Ontology
    • knowledge graph
  • Why it matters: Ontologies allow computers to reason over diverse, multi-modal datasets encoded in different languages or formats.

Philosophical Foundations: BFO, Realism, and Methodological Convictions

  • Explanation: Exploring Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), created by philosopher Barry Smith at the University of Buffalo, as the ISO-standard top-level architecture used across over 700 projects and government agencies.
  • Key claims:
    • Realism: Ontologies are designed to represent the world rather than simply concepts about the world.
    • Adequatism: BFO is non-reductive; classes and relations motivated by research communities are not paraphrased away.
    • Fallibilism: BFO is committed to tracking scientific research over time, recognizing that models might change.
  • Examples:
    • Distinguishing between independent continuants (material entities like tables or agents) and realizable entities (roles and dispositions like professor role or solubility).
    • Modeling Barry Smith as an instance of Agent, which is a subclass of Object, which is a subclass of Material Entity.
  • Terminology:
    • Basic Formal Ontology (BFO)
    • realism
    • adequatism
    • fallibilism
    • continuant
    • occurrent
    • disposition
    • role
  • Why it matters: Using a rigorous top-level ontology like BFO prevents ad-hoc modeling errors and provides guardrails for cross-domain interoperability.

Why Philosophers Make Good Ontologists

  • Explanation: Why philosophers possess unique skill sets in conceptual analysis, formal logic, and persuasion that make them highly valued and heavily recruited in ontology engineering.
  • Key claims:
    • Philosophers are not theory-laden or practice-laden within a specific scientific domain, allowing them to remain neutral.
    • They are trained to frame problems in multiple ways, identify subtle conceptual distinctions, and justify positions rigorously.
    • Philosophers excel at finding ontological solutions to messy domain problems, such as resolving ambiguity in virus definitions or pathogen dispositions.
  • Examples:
    • Resolving conflicting definitions of 'virion' and 'pathogen' among life science researchers.
    • Job market demand and 6-figure entry-level salaries for ontologists across finance, government, and tech.
  • Terminology:
    • conceptual analysis
    • formal logic
    • virion
    • pathogenic disposition
    • ontology engineering
  • Why it matters: Subject-matter experts often struggle with cross-domain conceptual clarity; philosophers provide the rigorous logical framework required for machine-interpretable data models.

Key Points

Big data problems stem from information silos, not just data volume

  • Explanation: Organizations struggle more with data incompatibility, proprietary formats, and lack of integration than raw storage capacity.
  • Evidence: NIST estimated lack of interoperability costs industrial datasets $21-43 billion; McKinsey estimates mid-size companies spend $20-50 million annually due to silos.
  • Practical implication: Computing strategies alone cannot solve fragmentation without semantic integration frameworks.

Realism over conceptualism in ontology design

  • Explanation: Ontologies should model the world as it is rather than modeling human concepts of the world to maintain coordination.
  • Evidence: Going from the world to words keeps researchers coordinated, whereas going from words to concepts leads to divergent definitions.
  • Practical implication: Ontology engineers must avoid subjective conceptual modeling and ground definitions in metaphysical reality.

Growing high-demand career path for philosophers in ontology

  • Explanation: There is a severe talent shortage of skilled ontologists across government agencies, financial institutions, and tech sectors, resulting in lucrative career opportunities.
  • Evidence: Job postings from organizations like Johns Hopkins APL, Morgan Stanley, Citi, and the University of Pennsylvania explicitly require philosophy backgrounds.
  • Practical implication: Philosophical training in logic and conceptual analysis translates directly into high-paying applied tech roles.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Basic Formal Ontology (BFO)

  • How it works: Provides a top-level ontological architecture with general categories (continuant, occurrent, material entity, realizable entity) that specific domain ontologies extend downward from.
  • Components:
    • Continuant (independent and dependent continuants)
    • Occurrent (processes, temporal regions)
    • Material Entity
    • Realizable Entity (roles, dispositions, functions)
  • When to use: When building domain ontologies that require rigorous interoperability, consistency checking, and alignment with standards like ISO.

Hub & Spoke Strategy

  • How it works: Uses a top-level hub ontology (like BFO) connected to multiple modular spoke ontologies representing specific domains via downward population.
  • Components:
    • Hub ontology (BFO)
    • Spoke ontologies (domain-specific modules)
    • Downward population hierarchy
    • Shared semantics guardrails
  • When to use: When integrating disparate data sources and ensuring consistent cross-domain validation and interoperability upfront.

Examples & Case Studies

Life science researchers used a Linnean taxonomy to classify viruses, resulting in a monstrous and messy hierarchy where viruses like HIV ended up classified under human patient subcategories.

  • Illustrates: The inadequacy of ad-hoc or domain-biased taxonomies for complex data modeling.
  • Lesson: Philosophical training helps identify subtle distinctions and propose cleaner classification models, such as adopting the Baltimore classification or disposition-based pathogen models.

A UB philosophy graduate student went to a conference with John Beverley, met his former boss at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab in the bathroom, and walked out with a job offer in 3 minutes.

  • Illustrates: The extreme market demand and high employability of philosophy graduates with ontology training.
  • Lesson: Ontology skills are so scarce and valuable that qualified candidates receive rapid hiring interest.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Read 'Semantic Web for the Working Ontologist' as a foundational text.
    • Participate in open NCOR ontology training sessions and working groups.
    • Create a GitHub account to track ontology artifacts, issues, and contributions.
  • Strategic:
    • Adopt BFO and realist ontology principles to future-proof data integration projects.
    • Recognize that generative AI highlights the necessity of rigorous semantic layers and formal logic rather than replacing them.
    • Position philosophical training as a high-value asset in tech and data science job markets.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can ontologies better integrate with machine learning models and large language models?
    • What are the precise boundaries between descriptive logic and first-order logic in practical ontology development?
    • How can government agencies accelerate the adoption of standardized core ontologies across disparate departments?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • As of 2022, over 147 zettabytes of data had been stored globally. (statistic)
  • Lack of interoperability across industrial datasets costs companies between $21-43 billion (NIST report). (report finding)
  • Mid-size companies spend 20-50 million dollars annually due to information silos (McKinsey estimate). (report finding)
  • Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) is the only ISO standard for top-level ontology development. (standardization fact)

Notable Quotes

"How philosophers provide a lot of value in the field that I work in, building ontologies and using them." (at 0:29) "Ontologies are known solutions to information silo challenges in the context of Big Data." (at 16:40) "Ontologies are formally well-defined machine-interpretable controlled vocabularies designed to represent entities and logical relationships among them." (at 16:52) "Computers are dumb and they do exactly what you tell them and no more or no less." (at 42:26) "If we attempt to go from the words we use to the world, it is unlikely that we will end up in the same place. If we attempt to go from the world to the words we use, it is more likely we will remain coordinated." (at 34:15)

Compressed Summary

  • Big data creates massive interoperability costs due to information silos and unstructured semantics.
  • Ontologies provide formally defined, machine-interpretable semantic layers acting as a lingua franca across data silos.
  • Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) relies on philosophical realism, adequatism, and fallibilism to model the real world.
  • Philosophers excel in ontology engineering because of their rigorous training in conceptual analysis, formal logic, and neutral problem framing.
  • There is an exploding job market and high demand for trained ontologists across government, finance, and technology.
  • Keywords: ontology, bfo, big data, interoperability, philosophy, semantic web
  • Core insight: Applying philosophical realism and formal ontology engineering to big data solves the trillion-dollar interoperability problem caused by information silos.

## Topic Map
### Big Data Problems and Information Silos
- **Explanation**: Examining the challenges of big data, including huge volume (over 147 zettabytes stored by 2022), high velocity, variety of formats (JSON-LD, XML), and veracity issues leading to conflicting data and information silos that cannot be easily integrated.
- **Key claims**:
  - Data is growing exponentially, making manual integration and human creativity insufficient.
  - Information silos cause data fragmentation, redundancy, bottlenecks, and incompatibility across repositories.
  - Lack of interoperability costs industrial datasets between $21-43 billion, with mid-size companies spending $20-50 million annually.
- **Examples**:
  - Data stored in docx files or text files in one database versus another incompatible system.
  - Disagreements between trusted academic journal articles or philosophical debates creating conflicting data.
- **Terminology**:
  - information silos
  - interoperability
  - zettabytes
  - data fragmentation
  - veracity
- **Why it matters**: Information silos prevent organizations from extracting true value from data, leading to massive financial waste and operational bottlenecks.
### Ontology Solutions and the Promise of Ontology Engineering
- **Explanation**: Ontologies serve as known solutions to information silo challenges by acting as formally well-defined, machine-interpretable controlled vocabularies that make implicit meanings explicit and provide a semantic layer.
- **Key claims**:
  - Ontologies provide a lingua franca across silos, reducing fragmentation and redundancy.
  - They promote automated data integration, standardizing querying and mapping.
  - Ontologies hit all five 'V's of big data: volume, velocity, variety, veracity, and value.
- **Examples**:
  - The Gene Ontology (GO) consortium, started in 1998 alongside the human genome project to coordinate biological terminology.
  - Government and industry adoption of ontologies in AI roadmaps (DARPA, DHS, NIST, Gardner).
- **Terminology**:
  - ontology
  - semantic layer
  - lingua franca
  - Gene Ontology
  - knowledge graph
- **Why it matters**: Ontologies allow computers to reason over diverse, multi-modal datasets encoded in different languages or formats.
### Philosophical Foundations: BFO, Realism, and Methodological Convictions
- **Explanation**: Exploring Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), created by philosopher Barry Smith at the University of Buffalo, as the ISO-standard top-level architecture used across over 700 projects and government agencies.
- **Key claims**:
  - Realism: Ontologies are designed to represent the world rather than simply concepts about the world.
  - Adequatism: BFO is non-reductive; classes and relations motivated by research communities are not paraphrased away.
  - Fallibilism: BFO is committed to tracking scientific research over time, recognizing that models might change.
- **Examples**:
  - Distinguishing between independent continuants (material entities like tables or agents) and realizable entities (roles and dispositions like professor role or solubility).
  - Modeling Barry Smith as an instance of Agent, which is a subclass of Object, which is a subclass of Material Entity.
- **Terminology**:
  - Basic Formal Ontology (BFO)
  - realism
  - adequatism
  - fallibilism
  - continuant
  - occurrent
  - disposition
  - role
- **Why it matters**: Using a rigorous top-level ontology like BFO prevents ad-hoc modeling errors and provides guardrails for cross-domain interoperability.
### Why Philosophers Make Good Ontologists
- **Explanation**: Why philosophers possess unique skill sets in conceptual analysis, formal logic, and persuasion that make them highly valued and heavily recruited in ontology engineering.
- **Key claims**:
  - Philosophers are not theory-laden or practice-laden within a specific scientific domain, allowing them to remain neutral.
  - They are trained to frame problems in multiple ways, identify subtle conceptual distinctions, and justify positions rigorously.
  - Philosophers excel at finding ontological solutions to messy domain problems, such as resolving ambiguity in virus definitions or pathogen dispositions.
- **Examples**:
  - Resolving conflicting definitions of 'virion' and 'pathogen' among life science researchers.
  - Job market demand and 6-figure entry-level salaries for ontologists across finance, government, and tech.
- **Terminology**:
  - conceptual analysis
  - formal logic
  - virion
  - pathogenic disposition
  - ontology engineering
- **Why it matters**: Subject-matter experts often struggle with cross-domain conceptual clarity; philosophers provide the rigorous logical framework required for machine-interpretable data models.
## Key Points
### Big data problems stem from information silos, not just data volume
- **Explanation**: Organizations struggle more with data incompatibility, proprietary formats, and lack of integration than raw storage capacity.
- **Evidence**: NIST estimated lack of interoperability costs industrial datasets $21-43 billion; McKinsey estimates mid-size companies spend $20-50 million annually due to silos.
- **Practical implication**: Computing strategies alone cannot solve fragmentation without semantic integration frameworks.
### Realism over conceptualism in ontology design
- **Explanation**: Ontologies should model the world as it is rather than modeling human concepts of the world to maintain coordination.
- **Evidence**: Going from the world to words keeps researchers coordinated, whereas going from words to concepts leads to divergent definitions.
- **Practical implication**: Ontology engineers must avoid subjective conceptual modeling and ground definitions in metaphysical reality.
### Growing high-demand career path for philosophers in ontology
- **Explanation**: There is a severe talent shortage of skilled ontologists across government agencies, financial institutions, and tech sectors, resulting in lucrative career opportunities.
- **Evidence**: Job postings from organizations like Johns Hopkins APL, Morgan Stanley, Citi, and the University of Pennsylvania explicitly require philosophy backgrounds.
- **Practical implication**: Philosophical training in logic and conceptual analysis translates directly into high-paying applied tech roles.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Basic Formal Ontology (BFO)
- **How it works**: Provides a top-level ontological architecture with general categories (continuant, occurrent, material entity, realizable entity) that specific domain ontologies extend downward from.
- **Components**:
  - Continuant (independent and dependent continuants)
  - Occurrent (processes, temporal regions)
  - Material Entity
  - Realizable Entity (roles, dispositions, functions)
- **When to use**: When building domain ontologies that require rigorous interoperability, consistency checking, and alignment with standards like ISO.
### Hub & Spoke Strategy
- **How it works**: Uses a top-level hub ontology (like BFO) connected to multiple modular spoke ontologies representing specific domains via downward population.
- **Components**:
  - Hub ontology (BFO)
  - Spoke ontologies (domain-specific modules)
  - Downward population hierarchy
  - Shared semantics guardrails
- **When to use**: When integrating disparate data sources and ensuring consistent cross-domain validation and interoperability upfront.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Life science researchers used a Linnean taxonomy to classify viruses, resulting in a monstrous and messy hierarchy where viruses like HIV ended up classified under human patient subcategories.
- **Illustrates**: The inadequacy of ad-hoc or domain-biased taxonomies for complex data modeling.
- **Lesson**: Philosophical training helps identify subtle distinctions and propose cleaner classification models, such as adopting the Baltimore classification or disposition-based pathogen models.
### A UB philosophy graduate student went to a conference with John Beverley, met his former boss at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab in the bathroom, and walked out with a job offer in 3 minutes.
- **Illustrates**: The extreme market demand and high employability of philosophy graduates with ontology training.
- **Lesson**: Ontology skills are so scarce and valuable that qualified candidates receive rapid hiring interest.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Read 'Semantic Web for the Working Ontologist' as a foundational text.
  - Participate in open NCOR ontology training sessions and working groups.
  - Create a GitHub account to track ontology artifacts, issues, and contributions.
- **Strategic**:
  - Adopt BFO and realist ontology principles to future-proof data integration projects.
  - Recognize that generative AI highlights the necessity of rigorous semantic layers and formal logic rather than replacing them.
  - Position philosophical training as a high-value asset in tech and data science job markets.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can ontologies better integrate with machine learning models and large language models?
  - What are the precise boundaries between descriptive logic and first-order logic in practical ontology development?
  - How can government agencies accelerate the adoption of standardized core ontologies across disparate departments?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- As of 2022, over 147 zettabytes of data had been stored globally. (statistic)
- Lack of interoperability across industrial datasets costs companies between $21-43 billion (NIST report). (report finding)
- Mid-size companies spend 20-50 million dollars annually due to information silos (McKinsey estimate). (report finding)
- Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) is the only ISO standard for top-level ontology development. (standardization fact)
## Notable Quotes
> "How philosophers provide a lot of value in the field that I work in, building ontologies and using them." (at 0:29)
> "Ontologies are known solutions to information silo challenges in the context of Big Data." (at 16:40)
> "Ontologies are formally well-defined machine-interpretable controlled vocabularies designed to represent entities and logical relationships among them." (at 16:52)
> "Computers are dumb and they do exactly what you tell them and no more or no less." (at 42:26)
> "If we attempt to go from the words we use to the world, it is unlikely that we will end up in the same place. If we attempt to go from the world to the words we use, it is more likely we will remain coordinated." (at 34:15)
## Compressed Summary
- Big data creates massive interoperability costs due to information silos and unstructured semantics.
- Ontologies provide formally defined, machine-interpretable semantic layers acting as a lingua franca across data silos.
- Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) relies on philosophical realism, adequatism, and fallibilism to model the real world.
- Philosophers excel in ontology engineering because of their rigorous training in conceptual analysis, formal logic, and neutral problem framing.
- There is an exploding job market and high demand for trained ontologists across government, finance, and technology.
- **Keywords**: ontology, bfo, big data, interoperability, philosophy, semantic web
- **Core insight**: Applying philosophical realism and formal ontology engineering to big data solves the trillion-dollar interoperability problem caused by information silos.
